title: Comparative Optical Spectroscopy of Er$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, and Eu$^{3+}$ Molecular Complexes at Cryogenic Temperature
authors: Farhad Rasekh, Sahil, Arsalan Mansourzadeh, Diogo Alves Gálico, David Hunger, Muralee Murugesu, Daniel Oblak
abstract: Rare-earth molecular complexes are attracting increasing interest for quantum information applications because of their structural flexibility and chemical tunability. Here, we compare the cryogenic optical properties of Er$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, and Eu$^{3+}$ complexes in the same ligand environment. Optical spectroscopy shows differing behavior across the three systems: spectral hole burning is observed in the Eu$^{3+}$ complex, whereas no measurable hole is detected in the Er$^{3+}$ and Tm$^{3+}$ complexes. We measure laser-induced local heating and rethermalization in the Er$^{3+}$ and Tm$^{3+}$ powder-like samples, observing strong local heating and slow thermal relaxation in the cold-plate cryostat. The recovery occurs over several seconds and, for some Er$^{3+}$ excitation conditions, extends over tens of seconds. The comparison across the three ions nevertheless suggests that heating alone is unlikely to account for the full contrast. Rather, the different behaviors of Eu$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, and Er$^{3+}$ point to ion-dependent relaxation and decoherence processes associated with their electronic level structure and coupling to the molecular environment. Temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift measurements are further consistent with phonon-mediated broadening through coupling to crystal-field levels.
summary: This paper compares the cryogenic optical properties of $	ext{Er}^{3+}$, $	ext{Tm}^{3+}$, and $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ molecular complexes to probe their fundamental relaxation mechanisms. By observing differences like spectral hole burning in $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ but not in the others, the authors argue that ion-specific decoherence processes are more important than simple thermal effects. The findings guide the development of better molecular designs for quantum applications.
main_problem: The study compares the cryogenic optical properties of $	ext{Er}^{3+}$, $	ext{Tm}^{3+}$, and $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$ molecular complexes to understand the underlying ion-dependent relaxation and decoherence mechanisms.
main_result: The differing spectral behaviors, particularly the observation of spectral hole burning only in $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$, suggest that ion-specific relaxation processes are more dominant than simple laser-induced local heating effects.
method: The research employs comparative cryogenic optical spectroscopy, including spectral hole burning, measurement of local heating/rethermalization, and temperature-dependent linewidth analysis.
model_or_system: The physical system consists of rare-earth ions ($	ext{Er}^{3+}$, $	ext{Tm}^{3+}$, $	ext{Eu}^{3+}$) incorporated into molecular complexes ($	ext{[Ln(acac)}_3	ext{(phen)]}$). Measurements are performed across different cryogenic platforms (liquid helium vs. cold-plate cryostats).
key_observables: Spectral hole burning presence/absence, local thermal relaxation time (seconds to tens of seconds), linewidth dependence on temperature and concentration, and crystal-field level structure.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures ($\sim 500 	ext{ mK}$ to $4.2 	ext{ K}$), concentration (1% to 100%), and the electronic structure of the specific rare-earth ions.
main_assumptions: The comparison is complicated by the different cooling power of the experimental cryostats, which limits the ability to perfectly isolate intrinsic ion behavior from thermal environment effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure, PXRD patterns, and FTIR spectra confirming the isostructural nature of the complexes.
paper_structure: The paper follows a comparative structure, first establishing the general optical properties of the three ions, then detailing specific measurements like SHB and thermal dynamics, and concluding with a discussion that disentangles the roles of heating versus intrinsic decoherence.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental issues in quantum optics and AMO physics by using lanthanides as solid-state quantum emitters. The comparison between different ions and the analysis of relaxation dynamics are crucial for designing robust quantum memory elements.
